events.place: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, Piazza Venezia 11, Rome
events.summary: Closing its ChatGPT inquiry with decision no. 755 of 2 November 2024, announced on 20 December 2024, the Garante fined OpenAI EUR 15 million and ordered a six-month information campaign on radio, TV, newspapers and the internet. It found OpenAI had trained ChatGPT on users' personal data without first identifying an appropriate legal basis, breached transparency duties, failed to notify a March 2023 breach and lacked age verification. The Garante removed the decision from its site.
events.significance: It shows both the reach and the fragility of after-the-fact enforcement: a EUR 15 million fine that covered training a model on personal data without a legal basis, annulled more than a year later over which regulator was competent - with the alleged violations never ruled on.

events.title: AI Act duties for general-purpose AI apply - including honouring machine-readable opt-outs
events.place: European AI Office, European Commission, Brussels
events.summary: From 2 August 2025 the AI Act's chapter on general-purpose AI models applied. Providers of models already on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027 to comply. The Commission's GPAI Code of Practice, published on 10 July 2025, commits signatories to crawlers that follow robots.txt as specified in RFC 9309.

The Commission can fine providers only from August 2026, and models already on the market have until August 2027. events.title: EU 'Digital Omnibus' proposes that websites must honour automated, machine-readable privacy choices
events.place: European Commission, Berlaymont building, Brussels
events.summary: The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837 of 19 November 2025, would insert Article 88b into the GDPR. Controllers' online interfaces would have to let people give consent, and refuse it or object, 'through automated and machine-readable means', and controllers would have to respect those choices (media service providers are exempt). European standardisation organisations would be asked to draft standards for interpreting the signals, and web-browser providers that are not SMEs would have to support them 48 months after entry into force. A proposed Article 88c would let AI development rely on legitimate interests, with data subjects given an 'unconditional right to object'. On 10 February 2026 the EDPB and EDPS 'strongly welcome[d]' Article 88b.
events.significance: Since 2016 the GDPR had let people object 'by automated means using technical specifications' without requiring anyone to build for it. This text would require controllers' interfaces to accept and respect a person's own machine-readable signals, and browsers to send them - the regulatory opening an IEEE 7012 agent needs.

events.title: IEEE publishes 7012-2025 ('MyTerms'): personal privacy terms that people's agents proffer
events.place: IEEE Standards Association, 445 Hoes Lane, Piscataway, New Jersey
events.summary: IEEE 7012-2025, Standard for Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms, approved by the IEEE SA Standards Board on 4 November 2025 and published on 20 January 2026, covers agreements between individuals and the websites, applications 'and AI agents' they deal with. Individuals act as first parties and point to standard-form terms from a roster kept by a neutral non-business body; if the second party agrees, both sides or their agents sign and each keeps a matching record that can be retrieved, audited or disputed. The project's PAR had been approved on 6 December 2017.

events.title: EU Council draft drops the machine-readable consent signal; 19 groups demand it back
events.place: Council of the European Union, Europa building, Brussels
events.summary: According to noyb, the Council compromise text of 18 June 2026 on the Digital Omnibus removed Article 88b, the proposed obligation to respect automated, machine-readable signals of users' privacy choices. The text was the Cypriot presidency's draft Council negotiating mandate. The COREPER vote on that mandate, set for 26 June, was cancelled, and work passed to the Irish presidency. myths.claim: IEEE 7012 / MyTerms is just another browser flag like Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.
myths.correction: DNT and GPC are one-way preference signals. The browser sends a single header value asking sites not to track, or not to sell or share personal data. IEEE 7012 makes the individual the first party who proffers standard-form contractual terms. The site accepts one, both sides (or their agents) sign, and each keeps a matching record that can be audited or disputed. MyTerms may travel in a browser header 'on the model of' DNT and GPC, but its legal form is different: an agreement with records. (The characterisation of MyTerms as an enforceable contract is the project's own and is untested in court.)

counterpoints.point: Earlier machine-readable privacy signals failed: Do Not Track was never made binding, and P3P faded; why would 7012 fare better?
counterpoints.response: The difference claimed is legal form. In its 2020 CCPA rules California's Attorney General did not require businesses to treat Do Not Track as an opt-out, leaving that to their 'discretion', because a required signal must clearly communicate an intent to opt out of sale. GPC did gain legal force where regulators said it must be honoured (California, Colorado, Connecticut and New Jersey by January 2025), although GPC 'on its own does not create any legally binding obligations'. IEEE 7012 is a contract with records, but it too needs counterparties willing to honour it. P3P's history is covered in other slices of this study and was not re-verified here.

counterpoints.response: The fight over EU Article 88b shows the risk. noyb says that, after lobbying spearheaded by Google, several Member States blocked the proposal and the Council dropped Article 88b from its negotiating position in June 2026. MyTerms expects Apple, Google and other large platforms eventually to add MyTerms functions, but says agents can be as simple as independent browser and website add-ons.

counterpoints.point: Key mechanics are left open or only sketched: the format and location of agreement records, how parties move between agreements over time, and which protocol carries them.
counterpoints.response: IEEE 7012 deliberately allows 'any protocol that serves the purpose'. It fixes what a record must contain, but offers header and JSON encodings only as informative examples, and states that 'Interoperability between systems is not a requirement of this standard'. MyTerms says the record format is 'an option left open', and that how parties change agreements is left to developers. A MyTerms-team individual Internet-Draft (draft-curtis-myterms-01, May 2026) proposes one concrete protocol: DID-signed JSON agreements, an X-MyTerms-Agreements header and a .well-known discovery file. But it has no IETF standing. At the project's May 2026 workshop, demonstration agents were shown while the open reference implementation was still being built. Auditability across vendors therefore depends on which protocol gets adopted. The project acknowledges that agreements will differ across jurisdictions with different contract laws.

It specifies a concrete protocol: JSON agreements with hashed Markdown texts, EdDSA/JWS signing with DID keys, three attestation levels, an 'X-MyTerms-Agreements' HTTP response header, a /.well-known/myterms-configuration discovery file, and endpoints for storing and retrieving signed agreements. It said a reference browser plug-in and an open-source reference implementation were still being built. The demo site anysiteorapp.com is public. The response is updated to reflect all this.

The point says record content is 'left open'. The full text of IEEE 7012 (free on IEEE Xplore, read for this check) partly fills this in. Cl. 5.2.4 fixes the record's content: terms, date, time stamp, identifiers and a unique contract ID. Cl. 5.4.4 requires identical, immutable copies and substitutable storage. Cl. 4.3 requires a version number or release date for each agreement. Only the format and storage location are open. The point is narrowed accordingly.

The standard itself supports the core of the counterpoint, and more strongly than the FAQ. counterpoints.point: A site's own terms of service may override a person's signal, and the IETF's draft AI-preference vocabulary itself says contractual agreements 'might override' statements of preference.
counterpoints.response: This cuts both ways. It is why 7012 frames the person's terms as a contract rather than a preference. The standard requires the person's agent to 'specify that the individual’s chosen terms shall supersede any Terms of Use (TOU) or Privacy Policy'. The IETF draft itself allows that an arrangement can 'explicitly say otherwise'. Whether that clause beats a site's click-through terms the person has also accepted is a question of contract law the standard cannot settle, and no court has yet tested it.

The response is wrong that 'which agreement prevails ... is a question the standard's public materials do not resolve'. The normative text of IEEE 7012-2025 is free on IEEE Xplore, and cl. 5.2.1.3 addresses this directly: 'The individual’s agent shall specify that the individual’s chosen terms shall supersede any Terms of Use (TOU) or Privacy Policy.' sources.note: Full text of the standard, free via the IEEE GET Program (PDF downloaded without login on 2026-09-23; document page https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11360682, DOI 10.1109/IEEESTD.2025.11360682). --check FOUND. Informative Annex A.1 (FOUND): 'If the Person_Agent does not find SD BASE-AT acceptable, then it communicates this and terminates the process as IEEE 7012 does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation.'

issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23). It only says that negotiation is 'outside the scope' of the standard, which is not the same as prohibiting it.

The action is wrong about what the merchant may do. It says the shop's agent 'cannot counter-propose' and 'can only accept one of the offered agreements or decline'. The normative text of IEEE 7012-2025 (free on IEEE Xplore) gives the entity three options in cl. 5.3.1: '(a) Accept the terms an individual presents from the structured and bounded list, (b) Respond to the individual with a single alternative set of terms from the structured and bounded list, (c) Reject'. Cl. 5.2.2 caps this: 'There shall be no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party.' Informative Annex A.1 gives an example: the entity counter-offers SD BASE-AT, and 'IEEE 7012 does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation'. So a single counter-offer of another standard-form agreement is allowed. Editing the text and further haggling are not.
Title 'no haggling' is broadly right but is sharpened to reflect the one permitted counter-offer.

agentScenario.title: Both agents sign
agentScenario.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. Each agent signs the agreement electronically on behalf of its principal.
agentScenario.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 abstract: if both agree, the agreement is signed electronically by both parties or their agents. The signature scheme (e.g. keys, verifiable credentials) is not specified in public materials.

sources.title: IEEE 7012-2025 (standard page)
sources.quote: If both parties agree, the chosen contract or agreement shall be signed electronically by both parties or their agents, and a matching record shall be kept by both sides in a form that can be retrieved, audited, or disputed, if necessary, at some later time--and which is available to do so easily.

agentScenario.title: Both sides record the same agreement
agentScenario.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. Maya's agent stores its copy in her personal records; the shop stores an identical copy. The purchase itself proceeds under a separate payment mandate (for example AP2's cart mandate), which records the price and items but not privacy terms.
agentScenario.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 and MyTerms FAQ: both sides keep identical records; the form and storage location are left open by the standard. Linking a 7012 record to a payment mandate is not specified in public materials.

sources.title: MyTerms FAQs
sources.quote: In addition, MyTerms requires that both sides keep identical records of their agreement, so compliance can be audited, and disputes adjudicated, should the need arise.

sources.title: MyTerms FAQs - What does an 'agreement record kept by both sides' look like, and where is it stored?
sources.quote: This is an option left open by the MyTerms standard, to maximize development choices.

sources.title: Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)
sources.quote: After the agent presents a cart with the shoes you want, your approval signs a Cart Mandate .
sources.note: Illustrates a payment record running alongside, not part of, the 7012 agreement.

agentScenario.title: If a merchant refuses, the refusal is recorded too
agentScenario.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. At a second shop that declines SD-BASE, Maya's agent records the refusal and, following her settings, shops elsewhere.
agentScenario.supportInPublicMaterials: MyTerms FAQ: the person's agent can record a refusal and keep track of it. What the agent then does is a product decision, not specified in public materials.

sources.title: MyTerms FAQs - What happens if a company says 'No' to my terms?
sources.quote: Your agent can record that outcome, and it or other programs can keep track of it.

agentScenario.title: Later: audit or dispute
agentScenario.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. Months later Maya receives marketing from a third party that appears to have her shoe purchase. Her agent retrieves the signed SD-BASE record to support a complaint to the shop or a regulator.
agentScenario.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 abstract: records must be retrievable, auditable or disputable. How a breach is detected, and which forum hears the dispute, is not specified in public materials.
